Title: Growing green spaces
NewsSummary: Planting school gardens provides green spaces for children and builds connections with nature.
NewsContent:
The story of urbanisation in Kenya is one of cautious optimism with 27 per cent of the population living in urban areas, a figure that is increasing by an estimated 4.3 per cent a year. In Nairobi, the emphasis on developing gray infrastructure has resulted in inadequate green spaces, and consequently, raised concerns for the amount of natural spaces children can access.

Amongst other adverse effects of urbanisation is the worry of food security in the city. Given an increased need for food production within Nairobi, urban farming is a viable aspiration for future employment. Despite the reality of youth unemployment, the EAI Kenya Youth Survey revealed that only 11 per cent of youth wish to go into farming or agriculture as a profession. Providing young students with links to nature by introducing farming or gardening in school curriculums could influence future endeavors of Kenyan youth and encourage involvement in environmental issues while providing green spaces for children.

In the East African context, the discourse around school gardens has been largely focused on childhood nutrition, but creative school grounds featuring green spaces provide added benefits. Besides bringing children closer to nature, the inclusion of outdoor activities in curriculums, can improve the overall student experience by increasing attention and academic performance, and reducing behavioural problems and stress levels. Children's exposure to nature in their early years is believed to have profound advantages on their own development, as well as prompting an interest in contemporary environmental problems.

A child's concept of the natural world is often shaped through tangible experiences, which means that less interaction with nature leads to lower environmental awareness and complacency when it comes to understanding the natural world compared to a built environment. Environmental awareness is also strengthened by sensory experiences. Children living in urban environments are believed to be disconnected from nature as their access to green spaces lessen. 

When children have the opportunity to engage in "hands-on" encounters with natural elements as a part of their school curriculum, their concern and interest in nature increases. Students who partake in environmental education workshops found them to be significantly more impactful when they were able to access natural elements as a part of the learning.  

Stimulating positive impacts of children's connection to nature is best initiated during childhood. Environmental education is believed to be more effective and sustainable if implemented before the age of 11; as younger children learn more effectively through direct sensory contact compared to older children. Thus, the primary school level is a suitable platform for experiential education. 

The Food and Agriculture Association of the United Nations (FAO) published a guide for setting up and running a school garden. In the guide, they note that school gardens encourage safe, sustainable agriculture while children learn business and entrepreneurship skills in the agricultural sector. Children are able to grow fresh fruits and vegetables right at their school which can then be consumed by students. Additionally, they note that school gardens can also increase student's respect for their school grounds and develop positive attitudes towards agriculture.

These benefits are exemplified at Michinda Primary School in Nakuru, where students run a successful School Garden Initiative that supports students' hands-on education in food, agriculture, and the environment. Additionally, students participating in the programme have excelled in their national examinations. The harvest from the gardens also supplement the school feeding programme, therefore, addressing aspects of sustainable agriculture and food security.


Kristin Swardh is an EAI Research Assistant, conducting research on child-enabling environments in Kenya.
